build_inputs.angles:
1. Open on the scarcity, because that is the whole reason this car exists: Ferrari built three 330 P4s in 1967, chassis 0856, 0858 and 0860, and a fourth car that was a converted P3 burned at Le Mans and was scrapped. This is not one of them. Lead with the number three and the fact that you cannot buy one.

2. The engine is the honesty beat and you must get it right from the listing, because Norwood has used several: different cars have a 4.8-litre V12 from a Ferrari 400 GT on six Webers, a 5.5-litre V12 from a 456, and a 575 Maranello V12 of around 500 horsepower, usually through a five-speed Porsche G50 gearbox. Read this car's engine and gearbox off the listing and say exactly what it is. The point to make is that it is a real Ferrari V12, just not that Ferrari V12 - this is not a kit car with something generic in the back.

3. What the real one was: a 4.0-litre V12 making 450 horsepower at 8,000 rpm, with three valves per cylinder - two inlet, one exhaust - and Lucas fuel injection, in 1967. Those are Ferrari's own published figures. Use them to say what the shape is a copy of rather than claiming this car makes them.

4. The race beat, and be precise because the usual version is wrong: at Daytona in February 1967 Ferrari took the top three places and staged a side-by-side finish to answer Ford's 1-2-3 at Le Mans the year before. But only the first two cars were 330 P4s - Amon and Bandini won, Parkes and Scarfiotti were second, and third was a 412 P run by the customer team NART. Do not say three P4s crossed the line together.

5. Why a recreation is the only version of this car anybody can actually buy, which is the real argument: of the three surviving cars, two spent years as 350 Can-Am cars and wear bodywork fitted later, and the last one offered publicly failed to sell at a high bid of just under ten million dollars - in 2007. So the choice is not between this and a real one. There is no real one for sale, and arguably no wholly original one left.

6. Cover the catch honestly and close on it. A Norwood P4 that sold on this site earlier in 2026 went for about 600,000 dollars and came with no registration document, so what you can do with it depends on your state - check whether that is true of this car too. It will never be worth what a real one is and it is not pretending to be. Close by asking whether 600,000 for a car that looks and sounds like a ten-million-dollar Ferrari is the best or the worst money in the hobby.

script: Three originals were built in 1967, and good luck buying one. On June 30, 2026, a Ferrari 330 P4 Recreation by Norwood Autocraft sold on Cars & Bids for $600,000. Its 5.5-liter Ferrari 456 donor V12 was rated at 436 horsepower and 398 pound-feet of torque. Not some generic swap. It's naturally aspirated, so there's no turbocharger or supercharger involved. Norwood hand-formed aluminum over a steel tubular spaceframe, rather than wrapping replica panels around an existing road car. No fiberglass body here. This one's reportedly chassis thirteen of fifteen recreations, with adjustable coilovers rather than a donor car's suspension. They go for about $600,000 today; would you buy the recreation when an original is effectively out of reach?

sections.Highlights: THIS… is a Ferrari 330 P4 Recreation by Norwood Autocraft, finished in red with a black and red interior. This 330 P4 replica is chassis #13 of the reportedly 15 recreations of the classic 1967 Ferrari racecar produced by Norwood Autocraft. Reportedly built in 2005, it features a hand-formed aluminum body over a steel tubular spaceframe, a Ferrari 456-sourced V12 engine, and a Porsche G50 5-speed manual transmission. A partial list of notable currently installed equipment reported by the seller includes 15-inch Tecnomagnesio reproduction centerlock wheels, Coker Tire reproduction Firestone Indy tires, adjustable coilover suspension, a straight-pipe exhaust system, working lights, vinyl upholstery, and a gated shifter. Texas-based Ferrari specialist Bob Norwood started building faithful replicas of historic Ferraris over four decades ago. Norwood’s P4 recreation combines a tubular chassis that’s similar to the original racer with an aluminum body and a Ferrari V12 from later models, including the 456, 550, and 575. Power comes from a Ferrari 456-sourced 5.5-liter V12 engine. Output is sent to the rear wheels via a Porsche G50 5-speed manual transmission.
sections.Equipment: A partial list of notable currently installed equipment reported by the seller includes: 15-inch Tecnomagnesio reproduction centerlock wheels Coker Tire reproduction Firestone Indy tires Adjustable coilover suspension Straight-pipe exhaust system Working front and rear lights and windshield wiper Vinyl upholstery Gated shifter
sections.Seller Notes: The seller states that the door windows are placeholders, and that custom removable windows are commissioned and will be included with the sale. Bidders should note that this replica will be sold with a bill of sale, and may not be registerable in all states, depending on respective Specially Constructed Vehicle laws. As always, it's the buyer's responsibility to perform all due diligence regarding titling and registering this car in their respective state prior to placing a bid.
